summary: Points out two problems that arise when NAT devices are chained or deployed so that private address ranges overlap. One scenario is multiple layers of NAT used with DHCP, and the other involves networks that connect to each other and clash on addresses. It describes the consequences for applications and administrators.

plainLanguage.summary: If two streets in a town use the same house numbers, mail gets confused. When many home networks reuse the same private addresses and get tangled together, devices cannot always find each other. This document describes those mix-ups.

questions: problems with nat and overlapping address space
subtitle: When private networks reuse the same addresses, unexpected problems emerge.

tldr.problem: As NAT devices have become common and cheap, networks often layer multiple NATs or combine private networks with VPNs. When different private networks use the same IP address ranges (such as 10.1.1.0), devices cannot tell them apart, breaking both direct communication and remote access.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC catalogs two scenarios where this happens: multi-level NAT hierarchies (one NAT plugged into another), and remote workers connecting via VPN to corporate networks that share the same private address space. It identifies the specific problems in each and offers practical recommendations.
tldr.outcome: The RFC does not solve the overlap problem but documents how systems continue to function despite it, and provides guidance to administrators on configuring devices to work around the conflicts.

today: RFC 5684 is an Informational RFC published in February 2010 and describes real-world NAT and VPN deployment problems that persist today. It has not been obsoleted and remains relevant guidance for administrators dealing with overlapping address spaces.

sections.title: The Address Space Overlap Problem
sections.content:
The Internet was designed with a single global address space: one public IP address per host, assigned by official registries. But in practice, NAT devices and private networks have become ubiquitous. Combined with slow IPv6 adoption, the Internet has drifted toward a hierarchy of private address spaces clustered around shrinking pools of public addresses.

Three forces drive this unconventional architecture: IPv4 address depletion, the perceived security and privacy benefits of NAT filtering, and the simplicity of plug-and-play NAT devices that bundle NAT with DHCP. However, when these devices are layered—a NAT behind another NAT, or a remote worker connecting to a corporate VPN—and all use the same private address ranges (such as 10.1.1.0/24), conflicts arise. This RFC catalogs those problems and offers recommendations to make overlapping address spaces work.
sections.plainLanguage: Cheap NAT boxes let anyone plug in a home network without setting up IP addresses manually. But they all use the same private addresses by default. When you chain them together or connect remotely to a corporate network, you get address collisions that break things.

sections.title: Multi-Level NAT Networks
sections.content:
In a typical home setup, a single NAT sits between the home network and the Internet. The NAT translates outgoing packets from home addresses (10.1.1.x) to the ISP's public address, and translates replies back. This works because public and private addresses are disjoint.

But when one NAT is plugged into another NAT (a multi-level NAT hierarchy), or when an ISP itself uses NAT to share one public address among many customers, private address ranges inevitably overlap. Hosts on private networks at different levels use the same IP addresses, yet packets must traverse multiple NATs to reach the Internet.

Client-server communication still works: a host on a deeply nested private network can reach a public server because its packets are translated twice—once by the local NAT, then again by the upstream NAT. But peer-to-peer communication breaks: two hosts on different private networks cannot directly contact each other using their private addresses, because those addresses are duplicated elsewhere. A host may end up talking to the wrong peer with the same private address. The RFC notes that with assistance from a public server, peers can still communicate by exchanging their public endpoints.

Additionally, mistaken host identity occurs when services advertised to customers (such as DNS servers) use private addresses that overlap with customer hosts. A customer receives the ISP's DNS address as 10.1.1.11, but connects to a customer host with that address instead.
sections.plainLanguage: If you chain NAT boxes, each layer translates addresses again. Outgoing packets make it to the Internet because they get translated at each hop. But incoming traffic and local connections get confused when two networks use address 10.1.1.10.

sections.title: Remote Access VPN Conflicts
sections.content:
Enterprises often use Remote Access VPN to let employees securely reach the corporate network from home, hotels, or partner offices. The employee's VPN client is assigned a Virtual IP (VIP) address from the corporate address pool so applications can identify and route to the remote user.

When the remote site (home network) happens to use the same RFC 1918 private address range as the corporate network (both using 10.0.0.0/8, for example), the VPN client faces a routing dilemma: packets destined for the overlapping addresses must be routed either locally (to the home network) or through the VPN tunnel (to the corporate network), but not both simultaneously.

The RFC identifies several specific conflicts: a DHCP renewal request might be incorrectly intercepted and tunneled to the VPN server instead of reaching the local DHCP server; a keep-alive ping to the local router might be redirected to a host in the corporate network bearing the same address; the assigned VIP address might conflict with an existing host on the local network. The RFC recommends two approaches: Split VPN (corporate traffic over VPN, all else locally) if simultaneous access to both networks is needed, or Non-Split VPN (all traffic via VPN) for maximum security. It also advises enterprises to assign global public addresses to critical corporate servers so remote workers can always reach them.
sections.plainLanguage: A remote worker's home network and the company network both use private addresses from the same range. The VPN client gets confused: should a request to 10.1.1.10 go locally or through the VPN? Configuration choices control which path wins.

sections.title: Practical Recommendations
sections.content:
The RFC offers five actionable recommendations, addressed to ISPs, enterprises, and VPN client implementers:

For ISPs using multi-level NAT: Assign non-overlapping addresses to services advertised to customers. Alternatively, assign global addresses to critical services to prevent customers from accidentally routing to a customer host with the same address.

For remote VPN clients: Configure the client to never tunnel packets destined for the local router or DHCP server, protecting bootstrap connectivity. This prevents the VPN from accidentally hijacking essential local services.

For enterprises deploying VPN: Use Split VPN or Non-Split VPN based on security requirements. Maintain at least two distinct IP address pools so a VPN client can switch pools if the assigned VIP conflicts with the remote site. Assign global IP addresses to critical corporate servers to ensure remote users can always reach them.

The RFC also notes that NAT vendors should conform to behavioral requirements in related RFCs (5382, 4787, 5508) to support hairpin translations—where two hosts on different private networks communicate by exchanging packets through the upstream NAT.
sections.plainLanguage: ISPs should use different addresses for critical services. VPN clients should never tunnel local router or DHCP packets. Companies should have backup address pools and use global addresses for important servers. This way, overlapping addresses don't break everything.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content:
The primary security risk in overlapping address spaces is mistaken end host identity. If a critical service (such as SMTP mail) has the same private address at both the corporate and remote site, a user on Split VPN mode might unknowingly connect to the wrong server, compromising message confidentiality. An attacker or ISP at the remote site could intercept the user's mail.

The RFC recommends that critical servers use globally unique public addresses to eliminate this risk. It also advises applications to use end-to-end authentication (not IP-address-based authentication) to prevent hijacking and denial-of-service attacks stemming from address confusion.

The document notes that security issues specific to DHCP, NAT devices, and VPN technology are outside its scope, but the overlapping address scenario amplifies these existing risks.
sections.plainLanguage: If both your home and your company have a mail server at 10.1.1.5, you might accidentally send your work emails to your home server instead. Use global addresses for important servers, and don't rely on IP addresses alone to identify which server you are talking to.
